channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Ransomware against food and agriculture is up 62%, and the groups doing it schedule around harvest — which has just started
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Food and Ag-ISAC figures, reported by Industrial Cyber on 3 and 8 September, put ransomware against food and agriculture at 227 incidents through July 2026 — a 62% rise on the 140 recorded in the same period of 2025, and enough to rank it the eighth most-targeted sector — and at 247 by the end of August. Qilin has been the most active group against the sector this year, with 47 listed attacks; Qilin, Akira, CL0P, Play and Lynx led in 2025. In a passage on Iranian activity against food security, the ISAC also states that federal agencies have confirmed attacks on internet-exposed programmable logic controllers used in processing lines and grain-handling systems. The finding that should change planning is the timing one. The FBI, as cited in the 8 September analysis, warns that criminals target food and agricultural cooperatives during planting (April–June) and harvest, and the September–November harvest window — when elevators, processing plants and cold-chain operators run at maximum throughput with the least tolerance for downtime — opened during this reporting period. The consequence argument is the other half, and it is the part that separates this sector from the rest of manufacturing. Loss of cold-chain and refrigeration telemetry forces product disposal regardless of whether the product was ever actually out of temperature, because compliance cannot be demonstrated without a continuous record. Compromise of production, quality or traceability data is treated by regulators as a food-safety event that triggers holds or recalls, not as an IT outage. This is analysis and sector data, not a report of a specific compromise; re-checked on 22 September, no named food or agriculture operator has reported an OT-disruptive incident since. What has changed is corroboration rather than impact: Black Kite’s 17 September report counts 1,183 ransomware victims across manufacturing and distribution in the first seven months of the year, and on 18 September Rockwell Automation extended its recovery guidance for controllers whose passwords were set by intruders to the Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs that run packaging machines and utility skids in this sector. Leak-site claims against two agricultural-equipment makers surfaced on 18 September without any company statement and are not carried here. - Food and Ag-ISAC “State of the Threat” report as reported by Industrial Cyber on 3 Sep 2026, and Industrial Cyber’s 8 Sep 2026 feature analysis (ISAC through-August count, FBI seasonal warning) — both re-read 22 Sep 2026 - Feature published 8 Sep 2026; underlying ISAC report 3 Sep 2026; ransomware figures cover January–July 2026 (227) and January–August 2026 (247)

item.title: [Critical] A China-linked actor emptied the code repositories of an industrial automation firm — SCADA and HMI tooling, not customer data
item.category: Incident — China-linked campaign (moderate confidence), confirmed compromise, SCADA and HMI source code stolen
item.description: Acronis’s Threat Research Unit published research on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting a critical remote-code-execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004 (CVSS 9.8, fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July); Acronis observed exploitation from 29 July to 4 August. The campaign scanned 1,386 self-hosted Gitea instances across seven countries and, per Acronis, produced 11 confirmed compromised targets in five countries — Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The two that matter to industrial readers are a Taiwanese industrial automation company, from which hundreds of repositories were pulled, including a SCADA/HMI tool, IoT platform integrations and a network sniffer, and a Canadian renewable-energy operator, where Acronis counted 22 exploitation sessions, internal infrastructure mapping, three SSH key entries planted for persistence and 61 database dumps. The actor installed a custom C++ Linux implant the researchers call JITTERLY, with more than thirty post-exploitation commands, and an embedded LD_PRELOAD rootkit, SIXZUT. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, based on language artefacts and tradecraft, and Acronis does not tie it to a known APT group; the apparent aim is espionage and source-code theft, not ransomware. No food or agriculture victim is named. The reason it belongs on this page is the target class: a food plant’s process knowledge does not only live in the plant. It lives in the machine builder’s and integrator’s repositories — PLC and HMI projects, recipe and batch logic, refrigeration control code, and the credentials commissioning engineers left in them. - Acronis Threat Research Unit report (primary, re-read 22 Sep 2026) — reported by The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber, KEV dates per the CISA catalogue; attribution assessed at moderate confidence by the researchers - Research published 13 Sep 2026; media reporting 14–15 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from 29 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] A North Korea-linked implant lived inside HAProxy load balancers, in front of every application and outside EDR’s view
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Vendor research, nation-state espionage implant on load balancers, no OT impact
item.description: Rapid7 Labs published research on 16 September on a previously undocumented Linux backdoor it calls TED, together with a tool named curlRAT, found embedded in HAProxy load balancers at a South Korean media organisation and a South Korean automotive company. Rapid7 attributes the activity with medium confidence to a North Korean state-aligned group adjacent to APT37. The implant sits where TLS terminates, in front of all the applications behind the load balancer, and Rapid7 describes it as generating no anomalous processes, no unexpected outbound connections and no log entries — it works by intercepting traffic that is already passing through, on a class of appliance that typically carries no endpoint detection agent. The purpose is espionage and interception; no production or operational-technology impact is reported and no food or agriculture victim is named. It is on this page because the same architecture exists at most multi-site processors: a reverse proxy or load balancer in the industrial DMZ fronting the historian portal, the MES web tier, vendor remote-access landing pages and cold-chain dashboards, built once by the network team and never put in the EDR estate. The point is the blind spot, not the attribution. - Rapid7 Labs threat research report (primary) — reported by Dark Reading; attribution is the researchers’ medium-confidence assessment - Research published 16 Sep 2026; victims are two South Korean organisations in media and automotive; no OT impact reported

item.title: [Medium] Ransomware against manufacturers is up 40% this year, and the growth has moved to Europe
item.category: Research — Vendor report, leak-site counts, no named food victim
item.description: Black Kite’s 2026 Manufacturing and Distribution Ransomware Report, covered on 17 September, counts 1,183 new ransomware incidents against manufacturers in the first seven months of 2026 — a 40% rise on the same period in 2025, and part of 5,237 disclosed victims across manufacturing and distribution since January 2023. The geography has shifted: the United States accounts for 412 attacks, still the largest single share at 35% but down from 52%, while Europe rose 85% to 369 (Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40) and the rest of the world nearly doubled to 402. Qilin leads the actor table, followed by The Gentlemen — a group with 142 claimed manufacturing victims by mid-2026, about 12% of the year’s total — then Akira, DragonForce and INC Ransom. About half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago. Distribution logged 95 incidents in the first half of 2026 against 196 for the whole of 2025. Two caveats matter before anyone quotes this at a board. These are leak-site and disclosure counts, which measure claimed victims rather than confirmed OT-disruptive incidents. And the report covers manufacturing and distribution as a whole: food and beverage production sits inside that population, but the coverage gives no food-specific figures, so treat the trend as directional for this sector rather than as a sector count. - Black Kite 2026 Manufacturing and Distribution Ransomware Report — figures as reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber; the report itself was not read directly - Reported 17 Sep 2026; figures cover January–July 2026 against the same period in 2025

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Food and beverage processors sit inside the manufacturing and business-services categories behind this record. The sector's own history — production stoppages that begin as IT events — is exactly the pattern the numbers describe. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For food and beverage the consequence is a safety one, not just a production one: a compromised control system that produces an out-of-spec batch or a cold-chain excursion becomes a public-health problem. The argument is that engineered limits — mechanical stops, independent temperature cut-outs, physical verification steps — do more than any detection tool. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Google’s threat group saw a credential-harvesting campaign run end to end by autonomous agents in under six hours
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Autonomous agent tooling in a live campaign
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor ran a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign using an autonomous multi-agent framework, completing it in less than six hours. GTIG also describes actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and co-opting victim cloud environments to run their own AI workloads at the victim’s expense. GTIG’s John Hultquist frames the takeaway bluntly: assume every threat actor is using AI in some capacity. For food and agriculture the significance is speed rather than novelty. Credential theft against corporate accounts is already the documented route into distribution, ordering and plant-adjacent systems in this sector, and a campaign that completes inside a shift compresses the window in which a lean plant IT team could plausibly notice and intervene. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting — as covered by The Hacker News - Published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Food and Ag-ISAC: confirmed attacks on exposed plant-floor PLCs, and a “shadow OT” estate nobody has counted
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Sector threat report, confirmed PLC exposure
item.description: The Food and Ag-ISAC published its State of the Threat report on 3 September, and the operational findings matter more than the totals. Federal agencies have confirmed attacks on internet-exposed programmable logic controllers running processing lines and grain-handling equipment; hacktivist crews such as Dark Engine have demonstrated they can reach HMIs controlling automated machinery, irrigation and temperature-controlled storage; and the ISAC warns that “shadow OT” — networked silo sensors, automated feeders and cold-chain thermometers added for efficiency and never inventoried — is growing faster than most teams can track it. On volume, ransomware against food and agriculture reached 227 incidents through July, up 62% year on year, with Qilin (47), The Gentlemen (31) and Akira (14) the most active groups, making this the eighth most-targeted sector. - Food and Ag-ISAC “State of the Threat: Food and Agriculture Sector Cyber Trends” report, produced with the IT-ISAC — reported by Industrial Cyber - Report published and reported 3 Sep 2026; ransomware figures cover January–July 2026; retained as the foundation for the top story, re-read 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A small-site managed switch joins KEV — 996 Zyxel GS1900 units already had their configurations and root hashes pulled
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, added to KEV 21 September, three-day federal deadline
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN — or wherever the management interface is reachable — run operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel fixed it in June, in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents, and its advisory carries no CVSS score. What moved it into KEV is GreyNoise’s 21 September report on a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed as a Chinese speaker, that exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands lead the count — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from a Western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and probed a long list of other products including Gitea, UniFi OS and Proxmox. GreyNoise infers an overlap with the Red Heron actor carried in the incidents section, and infers AI-assisted tooling from the iteration pattern; both are inferences rather than observations, and the cross-links to Zyxel’s own advisory and the KEV entry are the parts to rely on. The GS1900 is a small-office switch, which in this sector means the packhouse office, the depot, the farm shop, the weighbridge cabin and the cold store an acquisition brought with it. A switch whose configuration and administrator hash have been exfiltrated is not a patch problem; it is a rebuild-and-rotate problem. - CISA KEV catalog entry, GreyNoise Labs report of 21 Sep 2026 and Zyxel’s security advisory of 16 Jun 2026; the Red Heron overlap and the AI-tooling assessment are GreyNoise inferences and are labelled as such - Zyxel advisory 16 Jun 2026; exploitation observed from 7 May 2026; GreyNoise report and KEV listing 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 bypass in Cisco ISE — the box that decides which devices are allowed onto the plant network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited as a zero-day, KEV-listed, three-day federal deadline
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 10.0 in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker reach the web-based management interface, and Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability”. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — the interim control is infrastructure access lists restricting management traffic. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, a three-day window that has now passed. No attacker attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or industrial targeting is claimed; Singapore’s CSA issued its own alert on 21 September, and Cisco’s advisory remains at revision 1.0. Cisco’s hunting guidance is specific: search the ISE API gateway access log for the string “dummyuser”, and review the same log inside any support bundle. The reason it sits on a food and beverage page is what ISE usually does in these estates: it is the network access control and 802.1X policy engine that decides which laptops, contractor devices and plant machines are admitted to which VLAN, and it frequently underwrites the remote-access authorisation at the industrial DMZ. An attacker with administrative control of that policy engine does not need a plant exploit to reach the line. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA KEV catalog — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published 16 Sep 2026; KEV listing 16 Sep 2026, federal deadline 19 Sep 2026 (passed); CSA Singapore alert 21 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Seven new CISA ICS advisories and one update on 17 September, and the PLC engineering software is the one to read first
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA released seven new industrial control system advisories on 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. Mitsubishi’s CVE-2026-15688 is an authentication algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings rated CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions. The Modicon M340 advisory (-04) is CISA’s republication of a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that can cause a denial of service, rated v3.1 7.5 and v4 8.7, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70 with separate fixed versions for the Ethernet communication modules. NetBotz 5 (-05) carries CVE-2026-13336, an OS command injection rated v3.1 6.4 and v4 7.3, and CVE-2026-13337, a SQL injection, both fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) is exposed to CVE-2026-31431, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel privilege escalation rated v3.1 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, an excessive-authentication-attempts weakness rated v3.1 5.3 and v4 6.9; Schneider’s remediation is version 1.6. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues in an electronic logging device for commercial trucking, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) had not reached the public CSAF mirror at the time of writing, so its detail is not quoted here. For food and beverage readers the relevant pair is editorial rather than official: Modicon M340 is a common process and discrete controller on plant lines, and GX Works3 is the engineering software used to write and load Mitsubishi PLC logic — an authentication weakness there is a control-program integrity question, not only a workstation one. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 — CVE detail for -01, -02 and -04 to -07 from the CISA CSAF record; -03 not yet published in the public mirror and therefore not quoted - Advisories released 17 Sep 2026; ICSA-26-211-07 updated the same day; no 22 Sep 2026 batch was visible at generation time

item.title: [Critical] One firmware, three vendors: CVSS 9.8 flaws in the IO-Link masters that sit on packaging and process lines
item.category: Advisory — Shared IO-Link master firmware across three vendors, fixes available, no reported exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published three coordinated advisories on 16 September for IO-Link master devices built on a common firmware older than 1.7.4: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8 (VDE-2026-027), Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2 and ICE3 modules (VDE-2026-014) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 devices (VDE-2026-028), all three carrying the same set of about 20 CVEs (CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565). The two worst are rated CVSS 9.8: CVE-2026-27546, an unauthenticated bypass that grants administrator access, and CVE-2026-27565, which lets an unauthenticated attacker upload a malicious IODD device-description file that runs a shell script as root. Many further command-injection flaws score 8.8, and the set also exposes password hashes and SSH private keys. Phoenix Contact’s advisory credits Nozomi Networks. No exploitation is reported, and fixed firmware 1.7.8 is available. IO-Link masters are the gateways between the plant network and the sensors and actuators on automated equipment, which in a food or beverage plant often means filling, packaging, palletising and conveying machinery delivered by a machine builder. That is why the practical question is less “do we own these?” than “did our OEMs build them in?”. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-027 (Phoenix Contact), VDE-2026-014 (Pepperl+Fuchs) and VDE-2026-028 (Carlo Gavazzi) - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell extends its “password you never set” recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs on packaging machines and utility skids
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, fifth revision, no CVE
item.description: Rockwell Automation revised its notice SD1790, Important Hardening Guidance and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown, to revision 5.0 on 18 September, extending the hardening and recovery instructions originally written for MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers to the Micro820 and Micro850. The notice exists because of the FBI public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, locking operators out of their own controllers. There is no CVE: the guidance is to remove controllers from direct internet exposure, reach them only through a VPN behind a firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project files, disable the controller’s HTTP server where it is not needed, and stay on current firmware. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data; it widens the population the recovery procedure is written for. The food-sector relevance is editorial but direct. The Micro800 family is the low-cost controller a machine builder fits to a case packer, a checkweigher, a CIP skid or a small refrigeration plant, often with the builder’s remote-access modem beside it, and it is precisely the class of device the Food and Ag-ISAC described when it said federal agencies had confirmed attacks on internet-exposed PLCs in processing lines and grain handling. Recovering a locked controller during a run means a stopped line and, in a cold-chain application, a product-disposition decision. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0 (primary), which references the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026; sector relevance of the Micro800 family is editorial assessment - Original notice 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026; no new Rockwell SD advisories 10–22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] ABB posts two advisories in two days: a missing length check in the Freelance DCS and a critical credential-reset flaw in dynovaPRO
item.category: Advisory — Vendor PSIRT, dynovaPRO at CVSS 9.1, Freelance at 7.5, no reported exploitation
item.description: ABB’s cybersecurity alerts page carries two new critical items dated in this window. On 18 September ABB published advisory 7PAA010706, Freelance — Missing Length Check, whose CSAF record identifies CVE-2023-5778 at CVSS v3.1 7.5; on 17 September it published 4JDE002044, dynovaPRO — Reset Credentials Vulnerability, rated CVSS 9.1 on ABB’s alerts listing. ABB’s listing page does not show CVE identifiers, affected versions or fixed releases, so nothing beyond the CSAF record is quoted here; read the PDFs before scheduling. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and no CISA republication was visible at generation time. Freelance is ABB’s compact distributed control system for process plants; where it appears in this sector it is typically the batching, utilities or CIP control layer at a dairy, brewery, sugar or edible-oil site rather than a packaging line. ABB’s listing gives no attack-vector detail, so treat reachability as unknown until the PDF is read; the dynovaPRO score is why the pair ranks above the routine advisory noise. dynovaPRO is a much narrower product, but a reset-credentials flaw in anything that fronts a control system deserves the same question: can an outsider reach the login page at all. The same ABB page also lists two 9 and 10 September advisories for the AC 800PEC family and Ability zenon relating to the Wibu CodeMeter licensing component, both rated 8.6. - ABB Cybersecurity Alerts and Notifications page (primary listing; advisory PDFs not read for this edition, so CVE identifiers and version detail are deliberately omitted) - dynovaPRO advisory 17 Sep 2026; Freelance advisory rev B 18 Sep 2026; CodeMeter-related advisories 9–10 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Three Linux kernel flaws entered KEV on 18 September — the kernel is inside the HMIs, edge gateways and IO-Link masters as well as the servers
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, KEV-listed, deadline passed, no attribution
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September that has now passed: CVE-2025-39964, a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto interface; CVE-2026-53266, an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling; and CVE-2025-39682, a flaw in kernel TLS zero-length record handling. No source found for this edition names the actor, the campaign or how the flaws are being used, and published CVSS figures differ between vendors and commentators, so none is quoted here. CISA’s catalog notes carry two warnings worth repeating: the affected kernel may be end-of-life in the product where it is found, and the component may be embedded in other vendors’ products. That second note is the food-sector point. The ABB Edgenius advisory in the 17 September CISA batch was itself a Linux kernel bug republished under an OT product name, and the same kernel sits inside panel-PC HMIs, cellular gateways at remote sites, the IO-Link masters carried above, refrigeration supervisors and the historian server. A KEV listing for the kernel is therefore a question for every OT vendor, not for the Linux administrator alone. Separately, on 18 September a researcher published working local-root exploits for four other kernel flaws; those are proof-of-concept only, are not in KEV and are not the same three vulnerabilities. - CISA KEV catalog additions of 18 Sep 2026 (two alerts) as confirmed through the catalog mirror and multiple secondary reports; exploitation detail and CVSS are not published consistently and are not quoted - KEV additions 18 Sep 2026; federal deadline 21 Sep 2026 (passed); separate proof-of-concept kernel exploits published 18 Sep 2026 are not part of the listing

item.title: [Medium] Moxa TN-4500B: an unauthenticated write in the web login knocks the switch over — fix is firmware 2.1
item.category: Advisory — Vendor PSIRT, unauthenticated denial of service, limited footprint in this sector
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in TN-4500B series switches running firmware 2.0 and earlier. An out-of-bounds write in the handling of the username field on the web login page lets an unauthenticated attacker crash the device, rated CVSS v4 8.8 with high availability impact and no confidentiality or integrity impact; the fix is firmware 2.1. No exploitation is reported. The TN-4500B is a ruggedised switch built for rolling stock and vehicles, so it is uncommon in a food plant, and this card ranks Medium here for that reason. It stays on the page because Moxa managed switches in general are common in packaging halls, cold stores and outdoor agricultural installations, and the shape of the flaw — a login page that can be broken before any credential is checked — is the same test to run on every industrial switch with a web interface: can anything other than an engineering host reach it. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 (primary); sector relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory released 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] mySCADA myPRO Manager flaw rated CVSS 9.8 opens management functions and the SMS alarm modem
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisory naming Food and Agriculture, fix available, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03, released on 15 September, covers mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. CVE-2026-73807 is a missing-authorization flaw rated CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567 is a missing-authentication flaw in a critical function rated 6.3. According to CISA, they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. CISA lists Food and Agriculture among the affected sectors, alongside critical manufacturing, energy, transportation and water. The fix is version 2.2, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. The SMS detail is the sector-relevant one: smaller processors, cold stores and agricultural sites often rely on text alerts for out-of-hours alarms, so a channel an outsider can write to is a channel staff may stop trusting. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 (CSAF record in CISA’s GitHub repository) - Advisory released 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch wave lands in the process-control layer that also enforces food safety
item.category: Advisory — September ICS patch wave, vendor fixes available, no reported exploitation
item.description: Schneider Electric and Siemens both shipped critical fixes on 8 September. The most consequential for food and beverage plants is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the safety variant is the part worth pausing on. Siemens published seven advisories the same day, spanning Reyrolle protection relays, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Both arrive on top of the 3 September Inductive Automation Ignition flaw, CVE-2026-77393 at CVSS 8.8, which sits in the HMI and SCADA layer of a great many processing sites. None is reported exploited. What makes this a sector story rather than a patch list is the point Industrial Cyber made on 8 September: in food manufacturing, process control is food-safety control. Cook and pasteurisation setpoints, chemical dosing, cold-chain holds and batch integrity all live there. - Schneider Electric and Siemens ProductCERT security notifications, CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-246-06 for Ignition — round-up reporting by SecurityWeek, sector framing from Industrial Cyber - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; Ignition advisory published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and food and beverage teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Food and beverage processors version recipe management, batch control integrations, MES and warehouse-management interfaces, and cold-chain telemetry code in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated reads against that repository expose both the process knowledge and the service credentials that reach packaging lines and refrigeration control. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s second SCALANCE LPE9403 study: 12 flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device
item.category: Advisory — Vendor-patched vulnerability research, chainable to root, no reported exploitation
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to 12 vulnerabilities — nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, scored between CVSS 5.3 and 8.5. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches; V4.0 HF0 and later carry the fixes. The finding that matters is not any single score: Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onto connected networks. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping straight, because the coverage has muddled them. The first part of this research, published 10 September, described four PROFINET DCP denial-of-service flaws rated CVSS 5.3 (CVE-2025-40575 to CVE-2025-40578) in a daemon that runs as root without authentication on every device interface. The underlying CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was an update to that advisory adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes, not a new critical vulnerability. Processing and packaging lines that use the LPE9403 to aggregate PROFINET data for MES or cloud analytics should read the chained-root result as the reason to close the firmware gap rather than defer it. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, parts one and two, and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 / CISA ICSA-25-135-18 — reporting via Industrial Cyber; the full 12-CVE identifier list has not been re-verified against Siemens’ advisory here, so it is not reproduced - Part one published 10 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 updated 15 Sep 2026; part two published 18 Sep 2026; underlying CVEs first disclosed May 2025

item.title: [Critical] A ransomware operator is picking encryption targets from inside Cisco firewall management — that is how a plant stops
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters. UAT-12197, unattributed, exploited CVE-2026-20079 and deployed a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials. UAT-11823, an APT cluster whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s, exploited both CVE-2026-20079 and the earlier CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant. UAT-11988, a ransomware operator, came in only through CVE-2026-20316 using static credentials, performed reconnaissance and compiled endpoint lists for encryption; Talos assesses with high confidence that its tactics are consistent with Qilin ransomware affiliates. On 16 September Cisco shipped the accompanying hardening release, advisory cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN: eight internally found CVEs, CVE-2026-20329 through CVE-2026-20336, up to CVSS 9.9, fixed across ASA, FTD and FMC. Food and beverage operators should read the Qilin detail literally. The sector’s production stoppages this year have followed that shape — enterprise intrusion, target enumeration, then encryption reaching the systems batching, packaging and refrigeration depend on. FMC is where the boundary meant to prevent that is configured. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; KEV federal remediation deadline 12 Sep 2026 (passed); hardening release 16 Sep 2026, revised 18 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The MikroTik router chain moved from disclosed to exploited — unauthenticated admin over SSH
item.category: Critical Advisory — Now confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS flaws known as the “MikroTrick” chain, previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited, are now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. This is a change of exploitation status, not a new vulnerability. It is on this page for the same reason the Cisco item is: the box sitting between a remote site and everything else is usually the cheapest thing in the estate and the least likely to be on anyone’s asset register. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber - Alert published 9 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from at least 2 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 10 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026 (passed); catalog re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC expects imminent attacks on two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws — patches landed 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre warned, in reporting published 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation attempts against two critical Check Point VPN vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both rated CVSS 9.8. They can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can also affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. Nothing is confirmed exploited and no public exploit code had been reported when the warning was issued — this is a forecast from a national CSIRT and is recorded as one. For a food or beverage business the exposure is the shape of the estate rather than the product: processing plants, distribution centres, leased cold stores and co-packers are usually stitched together by site-to-site tunnels on a small number of gateways, and the same gateways carry the OEM paths to filling, packaging and refrigeration controls. One gateway typically stands between a corporate network and every plant floor in the group. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer. Assessed as imminent; no confirmed exploitation and no food-sector victims named - Check Point fixes released 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A CVSS 9.8 flaw in Check Point’s management server hands root to an unauthenticated login request — the console that writes every plant’s firewall rules
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management plane, not exploited
item.description: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, rated CVSS 9.8, in its Security Management and Log Servers, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and in SecurityWeek’s round-up of 18 September. The flaw is a stack overflow in the login process: an unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can lead to code execution as root. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be confirmed in the vendor text, so treat it as reported rather than settled. Affected builds are R82.10 up to JHF Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, every R82.20 build (no protective jumbo hotfix yet), R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines. Multi-Domain Server is affected; Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. Check Point says there is no indication of exploitation in the wild. This is a separate issue from the two VPN flaws in the card above. In a food or beverage group, one management server usually holds the policy for every gateway — plant, distribution centre, leased cold store and co-packer tunnel — so whoever controls it can reshape the boundary between the enterprise and production networks without touching a gateway directly. - Check Point advisory sk1000155 — reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek; the vendor page itself could not be retrieved for this edition. No exploitation and no food-sector exposure reported - Reported 17 Sep 2026; SecurityWeek round-up 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV — including the tool your line OEM dials in with at 3 am
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 and 11 September after evidence of active exploitation, reported together on 12 September, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS and 14 September for ScreenConnect (both passed) and 25 September for Artifactory, which is this Thursday. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain carried separately here. ScreenConnect is the one that matters most on a food page. Filling, labelling, palletising and refrigeration vendors support their equipment remotely, often out of hours during a run, and the agent that makes that possible is usually installed at commissioning on the same PC that programs the line. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV additions 10–11 Sep 2026; reporting 12–13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13 and 14 Sep 2026 (passed) and 25 Sep 2026 (open)

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform that manages plant IT — plus two Windows zero-days and a Magento bug
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor patches already available. The one to act on first is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection issue giving pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. Also added: CVE-2026-81963 and CVE-2026-85880, both Windows privilege-escalation zero-days reaching SYSTEM, and CVE-2026-75650, a CVSS 10.0 template-engine injection in Adobe Commerce and Magento that Adobe confirms is being used against merchants. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able, Microsoft and Adobe advisories — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and CyberScoop - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The rest of the September patch wave: Siemens Reyrolle, Industrial Edge Management and hardcoded keys in Aveva
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patches available, no reported exploitation
item.description: Beyond the Modicon and Ignition items, the 8 September wave carried several findings worth logging even where the equipment is not on a food line. Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays, all versions before V2.70; the lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8, lets an attacker derive current and past session identifiers from data the web interface leaks and bypass authentication. Weak session entropy and a role-based access control bypass granting administrator rights sit alongside it. Siemens issued nine advisories in total, also naming Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager, and began shipping fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key and MD5 password hashing; CISA formalised those on 10 September as advisory ICSA-26-253-01 — CVE-2026-81821 and CVE-2026-81822 both at CVSS v3 8.4, CVE-2026-81823 at 5.3 and CVE-2026-81824 at 4.7, affecting versions up to and including 2025_SP1_P1 and fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. It was the only new ICS advisory CISA published in the 9–11 September window. None is reported exploited. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and the wider September ProductCERT set, with Aveva security bulletin AVEVA-2026-006 and CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 — round-up reporting by SecurityWeek and ISSSource - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026 (SSA-142885 v1.0); CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 for Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] HKCERT: patching an edge device does not evict whoever is already on it — assume breach at the VPN, firewall and router layer
item.category: Guidance — National CERT advisory on internet-edge devices, no incident cited
item.description: Hong Kong’s computer emergency response team published an advisory on 15 September, covered by Industrial Cyber on 21 September, warning that VPN appliances, firewalls, routers and remote-access systems remain the primary route into internal networks, and that patching alone does not remove stolen credentials or persistent access from a device that was already compromised. HKCERT recommends an assume-breach posture for internet-edge devices: multi-factor authentication on every remote path, credential rotation after patching rather than before, and monitoring for lateral movement from the edge into enterprise and operational networks. The advisory cites no specific incident. It is carried here as the summary line under the edge cards on this page — Cisco ISE and FMC, MikroTik, Zyxel GS1900, Check Point, the Linux-kernel trio — because the pattern across all of them is the same, and because the food sector’s edge is unusually thin: a single firewall or cellular router at a plant, a packhouse or a grain site is often the only boundary between the internet and the line. - HKCERT security advisory of 15 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber on 21 Sep 2026 - Advisory 15 Sep 2026; coverage 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA makes the case for decoys — a detection method you can add without touching the process
item.category: Guidance — Detection method for critical infrastructure networks
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The premise is unsentimental: assume an attacker will eventually obtain some access, and plant assets whose only purpose is to be touched by someone who should not be there. The guide covers tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens, positions them alongside Zero Trust rather than instead of it, and structures the work in three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — to be iterated with red-team exercises. Planning is framed around the three MITRE Engage goals of expose, affect and elicit, with detections mapped to ATT&CK and deliberate attention to the living-off-the-land activity that signature-based tooling misses. Industrial Cyber’s coverage reports a detailed water and wastewater case study in the document, including decoys placed to look like OT HMIs; SecurityWeek’s write-up does not mention water or OT, so treat the OT case study as that outlet’s reporting until you have read the PDF. The reason this suits food and beverage plants is the one thing decoys do not require: a change to a live control system. A fake historian share, a false engineering-workstation credential or an HMI-looking host on the plant VLAN costs no production risk and no vendor sign-off. - CISA, “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; the water and wastewater case study is Industrial Cyber’s reporting - Guidance published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether your process reads it
item.category: Policy — Source change for vulnerability management teams
item.description: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September 2026, reported on 17 September. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, alerts and advisories all continue; the change is framed as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in Binding Operational Directive 26-04 in June 2026. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. For food and beverage operators the practical question is narrow and easy to check: does anything in your vulnerability-management routine, or in a managed service provider’s, consume that weekly bulletin as a feed or as the trigger for a review meeting? Small and mid-sized processors in particular tend to have one person who reads a weekly digest rather than a subscription to per-advisory feeds, and a source that stops arriving quietly is worse than one that stops loudly. - CISA announcement as reported by SecurityWeek; KEV, alerts and advisories are unaffected - Reported 17 Sep 2026; bulletin retired 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Food and beverage processors are beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, unless they place connected products on the EU market themselves. The practical gain is faster, more consistent vulnerability disclosure from the vendors of line control, packaging and cold-chain equipment. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — your line and refrigeration vendors now have 24 hours
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with exploit and mitigation detail, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available, as well as informing affected users. It applies to manufacturers placing products on the EU market wherever they are based, with penalties up to €15 million. For a food or beverage processor this cuts two ways. Your filling, packaging, palletising, refrigeration and ag-IoT suppliers — many of them European — are now on a 24-hour clock, so you should hear about exploited flaws sooner. And if your group builds or badges any connected product sold into Europe, the obligation may apply to you directly. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules, and the argument that they pull staff off the response
item.category: Policy — Incident reporting burden, CIRCIA rules pending
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September counting, from GAO figures, 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: in the first hours of an incident, the people who understand the affected systems are the same people drafting duplicate notifications in different formats to different regulators on different clocks. The timing matters because CIRCIA’s implementing rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. A food or agriculture business feels this acutely if it also handles payment card data, holds regulated financial or health information, ships product to state agencies, or operates in the EU alongside NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act duties — a single ransomware event at a processing site can trigger several clocks at once. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO figures — reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA implementing rules expected to be finalised autumn 2026
